Perianal fistulizing Crohn's disease: emerging biology, therapeutics, and roadmap for precision treatment. Perianal fistulizing Crohn's disease (PFCD) remains difficult to treat despite integrated medical and surgical management, and no validated biomarkers are currently available to guide pharmacological treatment selection. Recent single-cell, spatial, and multiomic studies have identified immune, stromal, epithelial, and microbial features across fistula tissue and rectal mucosa, expanding the biological characterization of PFCD. In this review, we examine how these molecular advances refine the biological understanding of PFCD and inform the evaluation of current and emerging pharmacological strategies. We critically assess the efficacy, safety, and strength of clinical evidence across distinct therapeutic approaches. We also discuss how molecular insights could support biomarker development for patient stratification and treatment selection, alongside anatomical phenotype, surgical context, and standardized multidimensional assessment of fistula healing.

Building sustainable IBD clinical research units: a practical toolbox emerging from a Belgian multi-stakeholder initiative. Clinical research is an essential pillar of modern inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) care, underpinning therapeutic innovation, biomarker discovery, precision medicine, and improvements in healthcare delivery. However, while international initiatives have successfully defined standards for clinical care, comparatively little attention has been devoted to the infrastructure required to conduct high-quality clinical research. Consequently, research capacity remains highly heterogeneous across centers, limiting patient access to clinical studies and reducing opportunities for collaborative research. To address this gap, a Belgian multi-stakeholder initiative involving patients, gastroenterologists, research nurses, study coordinators, and clinical researchers developed a practical toolbox for establishing and strengthening IBD clinical research units. Rather than defining rigid accreditation criteria, the toolbox distinguishes between essential components required for a functional research unit and important but non-essential elements that further improve quality, efficiency, and long-term sustainability. Structured across 3 complementary domains (administrative, operational, and collaborative) this framework provides a pragmatic roadmap that can support centers at different stages of research maturity. Beyond describing the toolbox, we discuss the concept of research readiness as a hallmark of excellence in modern IBD care and propose a roadmap for building sustainable research ecosystems. Although developed within the Belgian healthcare system, the principles presented are broadly applicable and may support the development of research capacity across healthcare systems and disease areas.

Clarifying ribA-dependent survival under mild heat stress in Escherichia coli. Zhang et al. provide an informative electrochemical framework linking riboflavin (RF) to the response of Escherichia coli to mild heat treatment (MHT). However, the central conclusion that ribA deletion abolishes survival under MHT unless exogenous RF is supplied appears difficult to reconcile with the food-matrix experiment. We highlight how RF supplementation during mutant pre-culture and post-treatment colony recovery may obscure heat-specific dependence on endogenous RF biosynthesis, and we propose a factorial validation strategy that could distinguish general riboflavin auxotrophy from a specific role in thermal adaptation.
